overview: Bithynia was a Hellenistic kingdom in northwestern Anatolia, built by a local dynasty amid struggles with Alexander’s successors. The atlas shows only 300 to 200 BCE within its longer history. Its narrow outline around the Kocaeli peninsula omits important parts of historical Bithynia, including Nicaea. It is not a complete boundary survey or the later Roman province. Earlier and later everyday-life examples below are explicitly dated.

periods.title: The atlas century within a longer kingdom
periods.summary: Zipoites and his successors defended and enlarged a regional kingdom; Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia.

items.text: Bithynian rulers resisted absorption by the Macedonian successor kingdoms. Memnon credits Zipoites with victories over forces of Lysimachus and Antiochus. This account comes from a later historian interested especially in neighboring Heracleia, so it gives us a political narrative rather than an impartial royal archive.

Nicomedes I sought allies as well as soldiers. Memnon says Heracleia sent thirteen warships when he confronted Antiochus, but the opposing fleets withdrew without battle. A successful alliance could matter even when nobody won a spectacular sea fight.

Nicomedes also helped Galatian groups cross into Asia under a treaty requiring them to support him and his children. Their armed intervention strengthened his position but brought violence and plunder to local inhabitants. The kingdom’s growth had very different meanings for a ruler and for villagers.

Nicomedes I founded Nicomedia, modern İzmit, beside the Gulf of Astacus. Memnon places the new city opposite older Astacus. Building a city could give a dynasty a durable name and center; the two places should not simply be collapsed into one site.

Royal childhood could be dangerous. Near his death, Nicomedes named the young sons of his second wife Etazeta as heirs and appointed foreign kings and cities as guardians. His older son Ziaelas returned with armed support to challenge that arrangement. A family inheritance dispute became a war.

sections.title: Silver portraits and a readable royal name

items.text: A silver tetradrachm of Nicomedes I in the British Museum dates to about 278 to 250 BCE. It measures 30 millimeters across and weighs 16.47 grams. One side shows his diademed portrait; the other shows an armed seated goddess. Such a tiny object can preserve a king’s public image remarkably well.

The coin type bears the Greek legend ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΝΙΚΟΜΗΔΟΥ, transliterated Basileōs Nikomēdou: “of King Nicomedes.” This is the scholarly catalogue’s normalized transcription of a third-century BCE royal coin legend. Greek lettering demonstrates the language of this official object; it does not establish what every household spoke or who could read.

For an earlier glimpse of the countryside, Xenophon describes the Calpe harbor region around 400 BCE, about a century before this map begins. He lists villages growing wheat, barley, beans, millet, sesame, figs and grapes for sweet wine. His army’s account records a varied farming landscape, not just palaces and fortresses.

Xenophon also describes local people moving property and enslaved people away while his soldiers took food from the countryside. Later, traders brought provisions to the army’s coastal camp. These passages show both exchange and coercion. The source rarely lets the affected villagers speak for themselves.

A comic story preserved by Athenaeus gives a king named Nicomedes a craving for anchovies far from the sea. His cook cuts a turnip into fish shapes and seasons it with oil, salt and poppy seeds. Vegetable disguise saves dinner! This is an undated literary joke about a Bithynian king, not proof of an everyday recipe.

Herophilus of Chalcedon worked in Alexandria in the early third century BCE. He distinguished nerves as a bodily system and connected them with the brain, sensation and movement. His work links the region with major medical inquiry abroad. It does not tell us what treatment an ordinary Bithynian child could obtain.

sections.title: Archaeology and life after the kings

items.text: At Üçtepeler near İzmit, the municipal guide records seven burial mounds, two excavated by the museum. The Aytepe tomb dates to the late Hellenistic or early Roman period, later than this map’s century. The larger excavated mound had already been robbed in antiquity. Calling these possible royal tombs does not identify their occupants.

The best-known local water complaint here is much later: under Emperor Trajan, Pliny reported that Nicomedia had spent heavily on two unfinished aqueducts. He proposed using surviving stonework in a new scheme. This is Roman evidence; it cannot supply missing details about third-century BCE toilets, household sanitation or water access.

ending.text: The map stops at 200 BCE, but the kingdom continued. In the conventional chronology, Nicomedes IV’s bequest brought Bithynia under Rome in 74 BCE, followed by conflict with Mithridates of Pontus. Royal sovereignty ended; cities and communities continued under new government. Roman Bithynia belongs to a different political phase.
